rv.q: The questions then become confused, the metaphors impenetrable, and the issue of who is the criminal, who the prisoner and who the observed becomes convoluted beyond resolution or care.
Sad to say, this thin and philosophically opaque work is pretty deadly too.
The surrealism feels lazy and the humour is unsatisfying.

Brook and Estienne's exploration of justice seems to be a half-baked melting pot, full of interesting snapshots, but results in a piece that, despite its swift 70-minute running time, lingers a little too long on the surface without digging deeper.

Despite its minimalist, philosophical flavour, The Prisoner smacks of narcissism: a play by a great absentee master of the British stage we can go and see and feel we have been in the presence of 'high' art. Missable.
This play is beautifully acted and holds concentration on and in every moment.
The Prisoner is self-indulgent and lacks the skill to convince the audience to be equally obsessed by its moral thrashing.

cn.t: Peter Brook's minimalist meditation on justice and punishment garners mixed-to-negative reviews, with critics finding it more thought experiment than compelling theatre, though some praise the performances.
